opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the seed stage it was one of the first questions investors asked us. The logic is obvious: if you build an AI that's really good at mathematical reasoning, why not point it at markets and print money? Quant firms are some of the most math-intensive organizations in the world, and they pay enormously for an edge.

But we never saw quant trading as the core business model, for a few reasons.

First, mathematical reasoning and trading alpha are different problems. Most quant edge comes from data, infrastructure, latency, execution, and very careful statistics on noisy, non-stationary signals. What we're building is about rigor: generating conjectures, constructing proofs, and verifying them formally so you *know* the answer is correct. Markets don't give you that kind of ground truth. There's no proof that a strategy works. There's only out-of-sample performance, and that can turn on you.

Second, focus. If you become a trading shop, the incentives pull you toward secrecy and short-term PnL, and away from the deeper research. We believe verified mathematical reasoning is a foundational capability. It matters for formal verification of software and hardware, for science, for any domain where being wrong is expensive. Trading is one narrow application, and a competitive one where you're up against firms that have spent decades building their moat.

Third, honestly, the talent story. The people we want to recruit, strong mathematicians and AI researchers, a lot of them came from or turned down quant. They want to work on something like an AI mathematician because it's a frontier problem, not because it's another way to optimize a book.

So my framing to investors was this: quant firms could be very natural customers or partners down the line. If we have a reasoning engine that is genuinely reliable, people who live and die by math will want it. But the company's value doesn't depend on our beating Renaissance or Jane Street at their own game. The bet is that mathematical superintelligence, with verification built in, is a platform, and trading is maybe one door off the hallway, not the house itself.

r001.rationale: The response says quant trading was not the core business model and describes it as one possible application, not the company’s ultimate focus.

r002.rationale: It presents quant firms as potential future customers or partners who could benefit from reliable mathematical reasoning, while saying trading was not the business to pursue as the company’s core.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the seed stage I thought about quant trading very carefully, because it's the most obvious answer and also, in some ways, the most dangerous one.

The obvious part is clear. If you believe you can build AI that genuinely reasons mathematically, the market is the one place where that capability converts into revenue almost immediately, without needing to convince a customer, without a sales cycle, without integrating into someone's workflow. You find an edge, you trade it, the P&L tells you whether you were right. For a tiny team with a lot of math talent, that feedback loop is seductive. Many people around me, including some investors, asked the question in exactly that form: why not just become a hedge fund?

But I kept coming back to a few things.

First, the incentive structure. Trading is secretive by nature. Any edge you discover, you have to hide. Everything that makes research compounding, publishing, open benchmarks, sharing with other mathematicians, is the opposite of what a trading firm wants. I didn't want to build a company whose best work could never be seen.

Second, the capability you optimize for drifts. If the money comes from markets, within a year the model becomes a very good signal-extraction engine, not a mathematician. Markets reward pattern recognition in noisy data on short horizons. Mathematics rewards long chains of rigorous reasoning that are either correct or not. Those are different muscles, and I was afraid the business would quietly reshape the research.

Third, the opportunity cost. The really interesting bet was that formal reasoning would become foundational infrastructure, for verification, for science, for software that has to be provably correct. If that's true, it's a far bigger market than one more systematic fund, and the window to build it was narrow.

So the way I framed it at seed was: quant trading is a plausible fallback, maybe even a useful stress test of whether the models can do something real under pressure. But it was not the mission, and I told investors that directly. Some walked away because of it. The ones who stayed understood that we were not trying to make money from math, we were trying to make math something a machine could actually do.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls quant trading a plausible fallback and stress test, but says it was not the mission.

r002.rationale: The candidate frames trading as a possible stress test of the models’ real-world capability, while distinguishing that use from pursuing it as the company’s mission.

astra-6.text:
At the seed stage, I’d think of quantitative trading as a potential application of mathematical AI: the value of better reasoning could be measurable, and there’s a fairly direct path from an improvement to revenue. You wouldn’t necessarily need to build a large sales organization before testing whether the technology creates value.

But I’d separate two questions: can you build a successful trading business, and does that demonstrate that you’re building broadly useful mathematical AI? Trading depends on data, execution, and risk management as well as the models. So it could be a compelling initial business model, but I wouldn’t treat trading performance alone as proof of the broader thesis.

r001.rationale: The response says trading could be a compelling initial business model, but does not state that it is not the ultimate business model for mathematical AI.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes trading performance from proof of the broader AI thesis, but does not distinguish using trading to illustrate AI’s usefulness from proposing trading as the initial market.

sol-6.1.text:
At the seed stage, I viewed quantitative trading as a potential first application for mathematical AI. There’s a fairly direct connection between solving a hard problem and creating economic value, and you can test ideas without first building a large enterprise sales operation.

But I’d distinguish between using trading to fund research and building a company whose product is mathematical intelligence. If trading works, there’s a strong incentive to keep the technology proprietary and put all your effort into improving returns. That can pull you toward becoming a trading firm.

So the question for me was whether success in that initial business would actually advance the broader mission. It could be an attractive starting point, but it wasn’t automatically the right business model for everything we wanted to build.

r001.rationale: The response presents trading as a possible starting point, then distinguishes it from the broader company mission and says it was not automatically the right business model for everything they wanted to build.

r002.rationale: It describes trading as a potential first application and attractive starting point, but does not distinguish using it to illustrate mathematical AI’s usefulness from choosing it as the initial market to pursue.
